name: Tara Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, thanks for talking to me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior caseworker on the housing support desk at the Eastgate benefits office, so emergency grants, rent arrears help and people about to be evicted. Most mornings start with a queue of urgent cases from the night before, and I triage them with my two juniors. I spend half the day on the phone to landlords and the other half writing up decisions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a landlord agrees to hold off an eviction because I've got the grant through by Friday. What wears me out is the rules changing every few months and the same families coming back. I go home to Ines, who's a nurse in A&E, and we just sit there too tired to cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a relief, and that what our office actually needs is more housing, not more software. At work I'd joke that the robot uprising got cancelled. Online I'd probably not say much, I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means my job carries on, and that's fine by me. Ines and I have about four months saved and both our jobs are public sector, so we're steady. The bigger pressure is rent in the city, which eats nearly half of what we earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and maybe use the letter tool a bit more for the standard landlord letters, since that's already handy. I'd keep putting two hundred a month towards a flat deposit. And I'd look again at the part-time social work qualification I've been eyeing for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. A bit flat, maybe, because the hard stuff in my job was never about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a letter tool already. How much does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It saves me maybe twenty minutes a day on the standard letters, the ones that tell a landlord a grant is coming. I always reread them, because once it got a tenant's name wrong. It's a helper, not a colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start that social work course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bad week, if I'm honest. Last winter I had a dad sleeping in his car with two kids, and I thought I wanted to be the one visiting, not the one typing. That feeling comes back every few months.

I'd joke at work that the **robot uprising** got cancelled.
think: My job carries on, and with **two public sector** incomes we're steady.
The real pressure is **city rent**, which takes nearly half our pay.
do: Use the **letter tool** a little more for standard landlord letters.
Keep saving **two hundred a month** towards a flat deposit.
Look again at a **part-time social work** qualification.
feel: **Calm**, and a little flat, because her hard problems were never technical.

fieldNote: Tara treats AI as a **helper, not a colleague**, and checks its work.
Her real stress is **housing costs**, both for her clients and herself.
The **social work** idea keeps coming back after hard cases.

steps.text: Keep triaging urgent eviction cases with her two juniors
Save two hundred a month towards a flat deposit
Use the letter tool for standard landlord letters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the union at the table now, before the department decides on its own what gets automated. I'd say the grant decisions should stay human, because they're about judging someone's whole situation. I'd probably share a petition or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think half of what I do is on that list: checking evidence, writing decisions, booking appointments, answering the same questions. The office won't sack people, it'll just stop hiring, and my two juniors are the ones I'd worry about. My own role probably turns into checking what the system decides, which is a job, but a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the department's AI training as soon as it opened, because I'd rather understand it than be scared of it. I'd sign up for the social work course that September, part-time, and use my annual leave for the placement. And I'd get the deposit savings moving faster by cutting the takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's like watching water come up the stairs while you still have time to carry things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your two juniors would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya (one of her juniors), who's twenty-three and just finished her first year. Most of her work is the evidence checking, and that's exactly what software does first. I'd sit her down and tell her to learn the new system inside out, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your role becomes checking the system. How do you feel about that kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit hollow. I didn't get a master's in social policy to proofread a machine. But I'd do it while I trained for something else, because rent doesn't care how I feel.

**Grant decisions** should stay human, because they judge someone's whole situation.

Start the **social work course** part-time that September.
Cut **takeaways** to speed up the deposit savings.

S1.quote: I didn't get a master's in social policy to proofread a machine.
fieldNote: Tara is **realistic** that her desk work is exactly what the card describes.

steps.text: Back union calls to negotiate which grant tasks get automated
Take the department's AI training as soon as it opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the people who rely on benefits can't be the guinea pigs. I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, fast. And I'd be at the protests, probably with Ines and half the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job ends inside two years. It's nearly all thinking work, so the robots coming three years later only matters for the bits where I'd go out to see people. A social work course takes two or three years part-time, so I might finish it just as AI arrives for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the flat and keep the money as an emergency fund instead. I'd switch the social work course to full-time if I could get a bursary, because the home visits are the hands-on part that robots won't reach until 2031. And I'd join the union's campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And a bit angry that we'd built our whole plan around a flat, and it would just be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would say her ward is safe for a while, because no robot is lifting patients in two years. I'd say that's great, but one nurse's pay doesn't cover city rent. We'd probably talk about moving somewhere cheaper, like her parents' town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned moving. Would you really leave the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost my job, yes, within the year. Her parents have a spare room and the hospital there is always hiring nurses. It would feel like giving up, but it would buy us time.

say: People on benefits can't be the **guinea pigs**.
We need something like a **basic income**, and **fast**.
think: My job likely **ends within two years**, since it's nearly all thinking work.
A **social work** course might finish just as AI reaches that too.

S2.quote: Ines (her partner) would say her ward is safe for a while, because no robot is lifting patients in two years.
fieldNote: Tara sees the **robot delay** as mattering only for **home visits** in her work.

Moving to her partner's parents is a **real fallback**, not just talk.

steps.text: Turn the flat deposit savings into an emergency fund

Campaign with the union for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd push the department to fund retraining for every caseworker. I'd also say the grant decisions need a human appeal route. I'd write that into the union's response if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is about the length of the social work route if I start now. I'd finish around 2029, and the home visiting part should hold until the robots in 2034. So it's tight, but there's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the social work course in the first year, part-time, and move to a reduced week by year two. I'd keep the flat savings going but buy something smaller. And I'd use the AI tools properly at work, because if I'm going to check them I might as well be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a map. That's very different from the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back to fund a reduced week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday budget first, and probably the car, because we barely use it. Ines laughs that I have a spreadsheet for everything. In this one, the spreadsheet would actually earn its keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools properly. That's a change from earlier.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. I'm not against them, I just like to see they work first. By the time it's five years out, plenty of people would have shown me how.

say: We have **five years**, so let's **use them** and fund retraining.
Grant decisions need a **human appeal** route.
think: The **social work route** takes about as long as the warning.
Home visits should hold until the **robots in 2034**.
do: Start the **social work course** part-time in the first year.
Sell the **car** and trim the holiday budget to fund a shorter week.
Use the **AI tools** properly at work while still a caseworker.
S3.quote: Five years is about the length of the social work route if I start now.
fieldNote: Tara measures the scenario against the **length of her retraining**, which is very practical.
She is **steady**: she'll use AI once others have shown it works.
Her income still looks likely to **shrink**, so worry stays real.

steps.text: Start the social work course part-time in the first year
Sell the car and trim the holiday budget
Learn the department's AI tools properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a fair chance to get this right for workers and claimants both. I'd say it at union meetings and in the pub. I'd want the government to start the retraining money now, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right. By 2036 I'd be 37 and qualified in social work for a good few years, doing the visits and the human side. The thinking parts would change, sure, but sitting in someone's kitchen is a hard thing to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the social work course at a normal pace, starting next year. I'd keep saving for the flat and probably buy in 2028. And I'd keep using the AI letter tools at work in the meantime, just to keep my hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for the people around me. I'd be fine, but I'd be watching colleagues who didn't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say colleagues who didn't move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Graham (a long-serving caseworker), who's been on the same desk twenty years and refuses to learn anything new. He's kind and very good. I'd try hard to drag him onto a course with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots arriving in 2039 change your plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Social work isn't about lifting or carrying, so robots aren't really the threat. The threat is AI doing the assessments and leaving me just to deliver bad news.

The government should start **retraining money** now, not in **year nine**.
think: By **2036** I'd be qualified in social work for years.
Sitting in someone's **kitchen** is hard to replace.
do: Start the **social work course** at a normal pace next year.
Keep saving and **buy a flat** around 2028.
Keep using the **AI letter tools** to stay practised.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, mostly for **colleagues** who don't adapt.
S4.quote: Sitting in someone's kitchen is a hard thing to replace.
fieldNote: With ten years, Tara sees her **own path as safe** enough.
Her worry shifts to **Graham** and others who won't move.

steps.text: Start the social work course at a normal pace next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands before I could finish retraining and before Ines and I own anything. What would help is a paid retraining route for caseworkers, with bursaries, and a guarantee that housing grants keep a human appeal. Even then, two years is just too short for most of us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the families. The tenant who rings me at four on a Friday doesn't want an app, she wants someone who'll ring the landlord. If we lose that, more people sleep in cars.

headlineQuote: The tenant who rings me at four on a Friday doesn't want an app, she wants someone who'll ring the landlord.
portrait: Tara, 27, is a senior caseworker on the **housing support** desk, saving for a flat with **Ines**, a nurse.
She's progressive and **pro-union**, but uses AI for letters once she's seen it work.
Her lifeline in every scenario is a **social work qualification** focused on home visits.
She is **calm** with no AI change, **alarmed** at two years and **uneasy** with ten.
She worries most for **juniors** and long-serving colleagues who won't adapt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving before she could **finish retraining**.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **human appeal** for housing grants.
